title: Akshay Kumar Just Sold Two Mumbai Apartments for ₹7.1 Crore. He Bought Them for ₹3.68 Crore Nine Years Ago.
excerpt: The actor's latest property deal in Oberoi Sky City, Borivali, reflects a 93 percent appreciation — and a broader lesson about Mumbai real estate for NRIs watching the market from overseas.
body:
The transaction documents tell a clean story. On June 2, 2026, Akshay Kumar sold two residential apartments in Oberoi Sky City, Borivali East, to a buyer named Suvarna Rupeshkumar Sakpal. The combined sale price: ₹7.1 crore. The combined purchase price, when Kumar acquired them from Incline Realty Pvt Ltd in November 2017: approximately ₹3.68 crore. The math works out to roughly 93 percent appreciation over nine years. No film career required for that return — just patience and the right postcode.

The details, sourced from property registration data accessed by CRE Matrix, break down neatly. The larger apartment spans 1,101 square feet of carpet area and sold for ₹5.75 crore, attracting ₹28.75 lakh in stamp duty. It was originally purchased for ₹3 crore and comes with two car parking spaces. The smaller unit, just 252 square feet, went for ₹1.35 crore — up from ₹67.55 lakh — with one parking space and ₹6.75 lakh in stamp duty.

## The Pattern, Not the Exception

This is not an isolated transaction. Kumar sold two other apartments in the same complex last year for an identical combined value of ₹7.10 crore, also purchased in 2017 for ₹3.69 crore. The consistency suggests a systematic approach to real estate rather than a one-off exit. He has been acquiring units in established suburban developments at relatively modest price points and exiting when appreciation reaches a certain threshold. It is more portfolio management than celebrity whim.

For an actor whose box office fortunes have been uneven in recent years — a string of underperforming films punctuated by occasional hits — the real estate moves serve as a reminder that Kumar has always been a shrewd businessman alongside his film career. His investments span property, brand endorsements, and strategic equity positions, and his net worth reflects decades of disciplined financial management as much as acting fees.

## What NRIs Should Notice

For the Indian diaspora, especially those who have been debating whether to invest in Indian real estate from abroad, Kumar's Borivali transactions are instructive. The western suburbs of Mumbai — Borivali, Malad, Goregaon, Kandivali — have seen sustained price appreciation over the last decade, driven by infrastructure improvements, metro connectivity, and the steady expansion of commercial hubs northward from traditional business districts.

Oberoi Sky City itself sits in what was once considered a mid-range suburban location. Today, it commands premium pricing, with Apple India recently leasing retail space in the associated mall for ₹2 crore in annual rent. The transformation of Borivali East from a residential backwater to a sought-after address has been one of the quieter but more significant real estate stories in Mumbai over the past decade.

The practical question for NRIs is whether similar appreciation is still available, or whether the easy gains have been captured. The data suggests the answer depends on the micro-market. Established projects in well-connected suburbs continue to appreciate steadily. New launches in emerging corridors along metro routes offer higher risk but potentially steeper returns. The fundamental driver remains unchanged: Mumbai continues to add people faster than it adds livable space, and the premium segment benefits from both genuine demand and investment appetite.

## The Stamp Duty Signal

One detail worth noting: the combined stamp duty across the two transactions was ₹35.5 lakh — not a trivial cost. For NRI investors, Indian property transactions carry additional considerations around tax residency, FEMA regulations, repatriation rules, and the practical complexity of managing property from abroad. Kumar, of course, lives in Mumbai and can manage his portfolio directly. Overseas investors rarely have that luxury, which is why many diaspora property purchases are driven as much by emotional attachment to India as by return calculations.

The numbers, though, are hard to argue with. A 93 percent return over nine years, in a hard asset, in a city that is not going to stop growing — that is the kind of math that makes even the most committed equity investor pause and reconsider.

Akshay Kumar's next film is *Welcome To The Jungle*. His next real estate move will probably be quieter, but no less calculated.
